Content:
Suppose we fix a basis [MATH: \mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}] of a finite-dimensional vector space [MATH: V] with scalars from [MATH: \mathbb{R}] (note that "finite-dimensional" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element [MATH: \mathbf{v} \in V] using the coordinates of [MATH: \mathbf{v}] relative to the basis [MATH: \mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; ⋮; x_{n}]]

Content:
This defines a bijective mapping [MATH: \phi: V\to \mathbb{R}^n.] Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:

Content:
- [MATH: \phi(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = \phi(\mathbf{u}) + \phi(\mathbf{v})] for any [MATH: \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V,] and
- [MATH: \phi(\alpha \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \phi(\mathbf{v})] for any [MATH: \mathbf{v} \in V] and any [MATH: \alpha \in \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
Because of this, we say that [MATH: V] is isomorphic to [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.] Intuitively, this means that [MATH: V] and [MATH: \mathbb R^n] have identical structures.

Content:
So, any finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] for some particular [MATH: n.] This means that instead of studying all possible vector spaces, we can simply study only one family of vector spaces, namely [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] for [MATH: n\geq 1.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We've already seen how to write the coordinates of a vector [MATH: \mathbf v\in \mathbb R^n] relative some general basis [MATH: \mathcal B] of [MATH: \mathbb R^n.] In this lesson, we will generalize this concept to abstract vector spaces.

Content:
As an example, consider the matrices [MATH: A_1] and [MATH: A_2,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [3|− 1; 0|5]]

Content:
The set [MATH: \mathcal{B}=\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}] is a basis of the vector space [MATH: V = \textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}.] Now, suppose that the coordinates of the matrix [MATH: C] relative to [MATH: \mathcal{B}] are

Content:
[MATH: [2; 4]]

Content:
Let's find the matrix [MATH: C] using this information.

Content:
As usual, any vector in [MATH: \textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}] can be written as

Content:
[MATH: x_1 A_1 + x_2 A_2,]

Content:
where [MATH: x_1,x_2] are the coordinates of the vector relative to the basis.

Content:
In our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}]]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: C|= 2 ⋅ [3|− 1; 0|5] + 4 ⋅ [0|3; 2|− 2]; = [6|− 2; 0|10] + [0|12; 8|− 8]; = [6|10; 8|2].]

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis

Example Prompt:
Consider the polynomials [MATH: p_1(t)] and [MATH: p_2(t),] given by
[MATH: p_1(t)=3+2t, \qquad
p_2(t)=-t+t^2.]
Find [MATH: p(t)] given that [MATH: \mathcal{B}=\big\{ p_1(t), p_2(t) \big\}] is a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1, p_2 \big\},] and the coordinates of [MATH: p(t)] relative to [MATH: \mathcal{B}] are [MATH: [4; − 3]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Any vector in [MATH: \textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1, p_2 \big\}] can be written as

[MATH: x_{1}p_{1}(t) + x_{2}p_{2}(t).]

In our case, we have

[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}]]

Therefore,
[MATH: p(t)|= 4 ⋅ (3 + 2t) + (− 3) ⋅ (− t + t^{2}); = 12 + 8t + 3t − 3t^{2}; = 12 + 11t − 3t^{2}.]

Item 5 — Example: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Matrix Vector Space

Example Prompt:
Consider the following matrices:
[MATH: [2|0; 8|− 4]]
If [MATH: \mathcal B = \{B_1,B_2\}] is a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{ B_1, B_2 \},] calculate [MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We need to find [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] such that

[MATH: x_1 B_1 +x_2 B_2 = A.]

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

[MATH: x_{1}[2|0; 8|− 4] + x_{2}[− 1|0; − 2|1]|= [− 5|0; − 2|1]; [2x_{1} − x_{2}|0; 8x_{1} − 2x_{2}|− 4x_{1} + x_{2}]|= [− 5|0; − 2|1].]

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

[MATH: {2x_{1} − x_{2} = − 5; 8x_{1} − 2x_{2} = − 2; − 4x_{1} + x_{2} = 1.]

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

[MATH: 2|− 1|− 5; 8|− 2|− 2; − 4|1|1]

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

[MATH: M =|[2|− 1|− 5; 8|− 2|− 2; − 4|1|1]|R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 4)R_{1}; R_{3}:=R_{3} + 2R_{1}; ∼|[2|− 1|− 5; 0|2|18; 0|− 1|− 9]]

The system is now
[MATH: {2x_{1} − x_{2} = − 5; 2x_{2} = 18; − x_{2} = − 9.]
From the second and third equations, we get [MATH: x_2 =9.] From the first equation, we get
[MATH: 2x_{1} − 9|= − 5; 2x_{1}|= 4; x_{1}|= 2.]

Therefore, [MATH: [2; 9]]

Item 8 — Example: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Polynomial Vector Space

Consider the following polynomials:

[MATH: p_1(t)=5+t^2, \quad
p_2(t)=3t-2t^2, \quad
q(t)=5-3t+3t^2.]

If [MATH: \mathcal{B}=\{ p_1(t), p_2(t) \}] is a basis of [MATH: \textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1(t), p_2(t) \big\},] find [MATH: [q(t)]_{\mathcal{B}}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We need to find [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] such that

[MATH: x_1 p_1(t)+x_2 p_2(t) = q(t)]

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

[MATH: x_{1}(5 + t^{2}) + x_{2}(3t − 2t^{2})|= 5 − 3t + 3t^{2}; 5x_{1} + 3x_{2}t + (x_{1} − 2x_{2})t^{2}|= 5 − 3t + 3t^{2}.]

Equating the coefficients of [MATH: t], we obtain

[MATH: {5x_{1} = 5; 3x_{2} = − 3; x_{1} − 2x_{2} = 3.]

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

[MATH: 5|0|5; 0|3|− 3; 1|− 2|3]

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

[MATH: M =|[5|0|5; 0|3|− 3; 1|− 2|3]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + (− (1)/(5))R_{1}; ∼|[5|0|5; 0|3|− 3; 0|− 2|2]|R_{3}|:=R_{3} + (2)/(3)R_{2}; ∼|[5|0|5; 0|3|− 3; 0|0|0]]

The system is now

[MATH: {5x_{1} = 5; 3x_{2} = − 3.]

From the first and second equations, we get [MATH: x_1=1] and [MATH: x_2 =-1.] Therefore, [MATH: [1; − 1]]

Item 11 — Tutorial: Isomorphisms of Vector Spaces

Content:
Suppose we fix a basis [MATH: \mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}] of a finite-dimensional vector space [MATH: V] with scalars from [MATH: \mathbb{R}] (note that "finite-dimensional" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element [MATH: \mathbf{v} \in V] using the coordinates of [MATH: \mathbf{v}] relative to the basis [MATH: \mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; ⋮; x_{n}]]

Content:
This defines a bijective mapping [MATH: \phi: V\to \mathbb{R}^n.] Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:

Content:
- [MATH: \phi(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = \phi(\mathbf{u}) + \phi(\mathbf{v})] for any [MATH: \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V,] and
- [MATH: \phi(\alpha \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \phi(\mathbf{v})] for any [MATH: \mathbf{v} \in V] and any [MATH: \alpha \in \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
Because of this, we say that [MATH: V] is isomorphic to [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.] Intuitively, this means that [MATH: V] and [MATH: \mathbb R^n] have identical structures.

Content:
So, any finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] for some particular [MATH: n.] This means that instead of studying all possible vector spaces, we can simply study only one family of vector spaces, namely [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] for [MATH: n\geq 1.]
